title: Phase 2 Pipeline Architecture and Plan
subtitle: XN task 1.4 sections | Will Daly | October 28, 2026
architecture: Our pipeline keeps the link between each molecule drawing, its label, and any table needed to build the complete molecule. This addresses the course project's central difficulty: scientific PDFs mix drawings with text, tables, and chemical notation (Northeastern University, College of Professional Studies, 2026b). The sponsor paper places the bottleneck on real papers in figure segmentation and in telling molecules from non-molecules, not in the recognition model: existing readers cannot abstain on a plot or table, and cannot combine a scaffold with tabulated R-groups (Gulluoglu et al., 2026). Our stages extend the pipeline that paper reports (Docling figure extraction, a molecule gate, MolScribe, RDKit canonicalization) with label linking and R-group assembly. Figure 1 shows each stage and its owner. The owners come from the team's planning issue; no member asked to swap by the October 20 deadline, so the assignments stand (XN Project Group 1, 2026a).

The front end renders page images and extracts native PDF text in parallel, detects candidate regions with MolDetV2, and applies a molecule filter. It keeps page coordinates and table context. MolGlyph reads each crop and MolScribe reads it a second time. A SMILES is marked high confidence only when both readers return the same canonical SMILES; disagreements and abstentions are kept rather than discarded. Label linking associates drawings with compound labels and table rows. Fully drawn molecules go straight to export, while scaffolds and substituents go to R-group assembly. When the evidence is ambiguous, the pipeline records an unresolved case rather than inventing a complete structure.

This design follows our evidence without assuming that detection performance on patents transfers to journal pages. The team table reports BioMiner at 73 of 220 unique internal molecules, with pooled precision of 67.6% and recall of 33.2%; the six-paper equal-weight values are 54.1% and 35.3% (XN Project Group 1, 2026c). No single reader run on the internal papers found more than 64 of the 220, because most molecules in papers 2, 4 and 19 are drawn as a scaffold with an R-group table or as separate fragments. Assembly and context handling are therefore the priorities, while detection and molecule filtering still need evaluation on journal pages. MolGlyph was the most consistent reader on BioVista, Patent300, CLEF, UOB and JPO, and two members' independent MolGlyph setups got the same 790 of 1,000 shared BioVista crops right (Adranly, 2026; Daly, 2026). Requiring MolScribe to agree raised internal-paper precision from 39% to 69% at a cost of 12 molecules (Daly, 2026). Neither reader's own confidence score separated right from wrong answers, so the policy relies on agreement instead (Adranly, 2026). These are baseline results, not results of the full pipeline.

We chose MolScribe over MolSight and MolNexTR as the second reader after comparing all four readers on the same 1,000 BioVista crops, using the members' committed predictions (XN Project Group 1, 2026b). As a second vote the three are effectively tied: keeping MolGlyph's answer only when the second reader matches gives 92.3% precision with MolScribe, 91.9% with MolSight and 93.2% with MolNexTR, each keeping about 430 of the 1,000 crops. MolGlyph's weak point is stereochemistry (Adranly, 2026; Jin, 2026). On chiral crops where both readers got the skeleton right, MolScribe had the stereochemistry right where MolGlyph did not on 23 crops, against 5 the other way; MolSight's split against MolGlyph was 22 to 16. MolScribe also already runs in the team's pinned environment, while MolSight needs newer packages than MolScribe allows and MolNexTR needs Python 3.8 (Adranly, 2026; Jin, 2026). Leaving both out removes the only reason for separate environments. Only 7 of the 222 internal answer rows have a stereocentre (Jin, 2026), so stereochemistry is evaluated on BioVista's chiral crops rather than on the internal papers.
plan: The whole pipeline runs in the team's pinned Python 3.11 environment (MolDetV2, MolGlyph, MolScribe, PyMuPDF and RDKit) and is driven by one script, so stages pass data to each other directly rather than through separate installations. Each stage also saves its output in the formats set by the team's interface specification, version 0.1 (pipeline/INTERFACES.md in the repository), for two reasons: GPU runs on the Explorer cluster can be rescored on a laptop CPU from committed files, and a wrong final SMILES can be traced back to the crop, reading, label or table cell that produced it. Each run records the PDF hash, package and model versions, configuration, hardware and source revision. Page and region identifiers follow a molecule through every stage, coordinates stay in PDF points, and records distinguish a rejected non-molecule, an abstention and a processing error. Tests check each stage's saved output against the specification, so a format change fails a test instead of silently breaking the next stage.

Peter builds the front end: page images, text, candidate crops, the molecule filter and raw table geometry. Bijay builds reading and consensus with MolGlyph and MolScribe, starting from the agreement rule above. Jin links labels such as 12a to drawings, scaffolds and table rows, and records the evidence for each link. Will builds R-group assembly and the export and scoring step, which writes the final predictions file and scores it with the team's existing scorer.

R-group assembly takes a scaffold reading with attachment points, plus the substituents that label linking ties to it (drawn fragments or table text), and returns one complete SMILES per compound or an abstention. A worked example on existing outputs shows both what the module can gain and its main risk (XN Project Group 1, 2026b). MolGlyph often reads a scaffold and its substituent as separate pieces, each with one attachment point. On page 3 of paper 4, for example, it read a Boc-protected PEG linker and a thalidomide end separately; joining them at the attachment point with RDKit gives compound 6 exactly. Across the six papers, joining every same-page pair of one-attachment fragments recovers 17 answer-key molecules that MolGlyph misses (15 in paper 4 and 2 in paper 19), which would raise its 64 of 220 to 81. The same procedure also produces 582 candidate joins, so pairing pieces blindly would flood the output with false positives. The 17 are therefore an upper bound that assumes perfect pairing, and the module only joins pieces that label linking connects. Paper 2 is the abstention case: its scaffolds come out with five unnumbered attachment points and the substituents sit in a table, so nothing yet says which column belongs at which position, and the module abstains until linking and table geometry supply that mapping. The first Phase 2 task for this module is checking whether MolGlyph's raw output keeps the R1 to R5 labels.

Already in place for this report are the interface specification, a CPU smoke run that renders paper 6 and writes every stage file with the model stages stubbed, the reader comparison, and the assembly example. Phase 2 follows the course schedule: each member implements and tests their module for tasks 2.2 and 2.3, due November 29, and the group integrates the modules for task 2.4, due December 13 (Northeastern University, College of Professional Studies, 2026a). We replace the smoke run's stubs one module at a time, starting with the front end and readers because they already exist as benchmark code, and score all six papers after each replacement so a drop in score points to the module that caused it. The team sync after each Tuesday class reviews those scores.

Evaluation compares the existing reader baseline with each added stage: filtering, consensus, linking and assembly. We report per-paper and equal-weight precision and recall, pooled results, output counts, and rejected or unresolved cases. Scoring stays exact match of canonical SMILES with no partial credit, as in the sponsor paper (Gulluoglu et al., 2026). Salt, tautomer and stereochemistry rules stay unchanged, and R-group labels are scored by one convention: two members' 0% Markush results came from how R-groups were written (* versus [1*]), not from misread drawings (Adranly, 2026; Chhetri, 2026). Because the six internal papers have already shaped the design, they are a development benchmark; claims about generalization need unseen papers, especially since reader rankings reversed between public datasets (Adranly, 2026). The main integration risks are tables that continue across pages, ambiguous attachment points, PDFs without a text layer, and false joins in assembly.
